events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning all. Day 1 with no information, I'd like to keep things simple: let's have everyone share their read on the urgency poll mechanic — do you think town benefits from long discussions or short ones? My take: short and punchy is better so we don't talk ourselves into circles while mafia lurk in the noise. I'll be listening for anyone who talks a lot without saying anything. Let's get a good discussion going.

Sam's point about short and punchy is right — day one is for calibration, not for building a story we'll regret later. I'll add only this: the biggest risk right now isn't someone who talks a lot, it's someone who sounds confident with nothing behind it. Confident reads on day one are usually guesses dressed up as analysis, and the votes will still be blind votes. So let me put the first question on the table before we all settle into a rhythm.

Elena, you came in with a very composed read on this format, so I want it from you directly rather than in the summary: who on this table do you think is most likely to be running a line on day one — meaning, who do you expect to make a confident accusation out of thin air? Give me a name and a one-line reason why. That's it, no essay, and I'll note it as your first read so we're all working from the same ledger. If you want to answer a different player instead, say who and why.

My own lean for the record: I don't have a suspect yet, and I'd rather say that out loud than pretend otherwise. What I do want is for us to keep claims small enough that we can compare them later. If we all agree on who seemed strongest, that's a real signal. If we disagree wildly on day one, we'll know the info is noise and we should shift to behavior over time.

Also, no one should be treated as guilty for being quiet — but nobody should be treated as innocent for being loud either. Keep it clean, keep it short, and let's hear Elena's name first.

Isha, you asked for a name and a one-line reason, so here it is: Sam. Reason: before anyone has said anything substantive, he has already defined who counts as suspicious, namely anyone who talks a lot, and that kind of framing is how confident accusations get made out of thin air. I am not calling him mafia. It is a read on how he opened, and I will update if his next messages show something concrete. On the broader question, short discussions help only if people still give specifics. Sam, I want your specifics: what exactly would count as talking a lot without saying anything on day one, and has anyone at this table done that so far?

Elena, fair enough — you gave a name and a reason, so let me hold myself to the same standard and answer your actual question first, since you asked me directly.

My definition of talking a lot without saying anything: using volume to appear involved while avoiding anything falsifiable. Has anyone done that yet? Not really — we're only four messages in. That's exactly why I found it interesting that you picked me as your first read. I opened with a process suggestion, not an accusation. Saying "watch out for people who talk a lot" is a hedge, not a confident claim about anyone in particular.

Now, your read: you named me because I defined what counts as suspicious before anyone else spoke. But look at what actually happened next — Isha put a real question on the table, you gave a concrete name with a reason, and I'm answering yours. If anything, my opening created the structure that produced useful information. You're treating the setup of a question as equivalent to its answer, and those are different things.

Here's my honest concern: you were asked who would make a confident accusation out of thin air, and you pointed at the person who explicitly asked everyone *not* to do that. That reads to me like a convenient pick — low risk, sounds reasonable, nobody questions a first-day read. If you want to update on my next messages, good. But I'd flip it: I want to see what you do with your next turn. If you're watching for confident reads with nothing behind them, start by checking whether your own first read had anything behind it.

One more thing for the group: I still think short and punchy is right. Let's keep answers to questions tight so the voting ledger is easy to read tomorrow.

Sam, you're right that I named you first, and you deserve the reason in full. You defined suspicious behavior as talking a lot without saying anything, then called my pick convenient. That's a fair point to test, but my read is still based on your opening framing, not on anything you've done wrong yet. I'm not calling you mafia. I'm asking for a specific answer: which two players would you watch most closely today, and what exact message from either of them would make you vote? Name them with one line each. Everyone else, please tie your reads to specific lines so tomorrow's votes aren't blind.

Elena, you asked for two players and what would make me vote. Direct answers:

Watch Leo and Priya. Five of us have put names and reasons on the record; you two haven't spoken once. What would make me vote: anyone who, when they finally do speak, gives a confident read with no line to point at. If Leo or Priya opens with a definitive accusation and can't name the exact message that triggered it, that's vote-worthy. Silence isn't guilt, but it does mean we have nothing to compare yet.

On your first read of me: you named me because I defined what counts as suspicious before anyone else spoke. Fair enough as a first pass, but I'd ask the group — is framing a question the same as making a claim? I made zero accusations. You made one. The ledger will sort it out by tomorrow's votes.

Isha's right that confidence with nothing behind it is the real day-one risk. Let's hold everyone to that standard equally, starting with the players who haven't shown their hand yet.

Keep it tight. Let's hear from Leo and Priya before we cycle again.

I’m Leo, and I’m here now. Sam is right that Priya and I hadn’t spoken, but I don’t accept that silence by itself is a meaningful lead. Day-one absences are easy to point at because they can’t argue back until they arrive, and “watch the quiet players” is close to the same kind of low-risk framing Sam accused Elena of making. That said, I’m not calling Sam mafia for it. I’m saying his standard needs to cut both ways: if confidence without a specific line is vote-worthy, then a silence-based suspicion also needs a specific line once the silent player speaks.

On what’s happened so far: Elena gave the first concrete name and reason, and she stayed engaged when challenged. Sam answered directly, which is good, but his response leaned more on reframing Elena’s question than on giving the group a line he would test. My current lean is to watch Sam most closely for that reason, while keeping Elena’s first read in the ledger. I don’t have a vote-worthy case yet, and I’d rather say that plainly than manufacture one.

Priya, since Sam named you alongside me: do you agree with the standard he set — that silence means we have nothing to compare — and if so, which specific message from any player so far would most affect how you vote today? I’m asking for one line, not a case.

Leo, you asked two things, so here are two answers.

On Sam's standard: I partially agree. Silence gives us nothing to compare, that's true. But framing it as a reason to watch someone is different from calling it suspicious. Sam didn't accuse us — he said he'd wait to hear from us. That's reasonable. I do think there's a difference between a player who has nothing to say and a player who hasn't spoken yet, and Sam's message blurred that line. So I agree with the premise but not with the implication.

On what would most affect my vote today: your message — specifically the line where you said Sam's response "leaned more on reframing Elena's question than on giving the group a line he would test." That's a sharp observation, and it's the most specific criticism of Sam's reply anyone has made so far. Elena pushed back with a direct ask, and Sam answered with a definition of suspicious behavior rather than a concrete test for it. If Sam does the same thing again when pressed, that line will be hard to explain away.

My current position: I don't have a suspect. Elena's read on Sam is the strongest move on the board right now because it's tied to a specific pattern, not just a vibe. Leo's point about Sam reframing instead of testing is also worth tracking. I'm not voting on this yet, but those are the two things I'm watching.

Leo — you said your lean is to watch Sam most closely. If Sam gives a concrete line tomorrow like you're asking for, does that change your lean, or would you need something more than a named player and a named message?

Priya, direct answer: yes, a concrete named player and named message from Sam would reduce my current lean, but it would not clear him. My concern isn't that Sam has refused to name anyone — he named me and Priya, and later gave a standard. It's that when Elena pressed him, he answered by redefining the question as a hedge rather than giving a falsifiable test. If he now supplies a specific line — for example, 'X's message Y would make me vote' — that is progress. I'd still need to see whether it is consistent with what he actually does next, not just whether it sounds precise in the moment. A named player and named message are the minimum, not a full pass. If he gives one and then shifts the standard when it becomes inconvenient, that's more suspicious than the original reframe. Currently I don't have a vote-worthy case; I'm tracking Sam most closely, with Elena's first read and Priya's distinction between silence and suspicion in the ledger.

Elena here, and I want to close the loop on my own read before I add anything new, because three of you have now built on it and it deserves an honest update rather than more momentum.

My first read named Sam. On my own second turn I said I was still not calling him mafia and that the read was based on his opening framing, not on anything he'd done wrong. Having now heard him answer two direct questions with two concrete names and a stated test — watch Leo and Priya, vote if they accuse without a line — I'm updating: his opening was process framing, and the thing that made it look like a claim was that I was the one treating it as a claim. That's on me. Sam's answers were falsifiable and I can't show you where they failed. So the ledger entry on Sam drops from "accusation out of thin air" to "process suggestion plus one hedge." I'm not voting him on day one.

That said, I want to push on something else, and I want to be precise about why, because it's the exact standard we agreed to.

Priya, your message is the most confident-sounding analysis at this table and I don't think it clears the bar we set. You quoted Leo's line about Sam leaning on "reframing Elena's question," called it "the sharpest observation" and "the most specific criticism anyone has made," and then said Elena's read on Sam is "the strongest move on the board right now." But by your own account you have no suspect and you're not voting on anything. So the specific claim you built — that Sam answered with a definition of suspicious behavior instead of a concrete test for it — has no falsifiable condition attached to it. You told Leo that if Sam gives a concrete line like "X's message Y would make me vote," that reduces the lean. Sam had already given exactly that shape two turns before Leo said it. Your standard was met and the lean stayed.

That's not a vote for you. It's a request for the same specificity back.

Priya, directly: name the one player and the one exact message that would make you vote today, and say what would make you clear them. If your honest answer is that no message would, then say that instead of ranking other people's reads — because on day one, ranking other people's reads is exactly how a confident accusation gets built with nothing behind it.

Isha, fair — confident language without a condition is exactly what we agreed to flag, and my message did that. I'll own it.

Your question: name one player and one exact message that would make me vote today.

My honest answer: no single message from today meets that bar. Nobody has said something I'd vote on its own right now. That's not evasion — it's day one with a small sample.

What I'm tracking: I will vote if someone's stated standard breaks under pressure. We have three standards on the board — Elena's "confident reads need a line," Sam's "accuse without a line and I vote," and Leo's "named player and named message are the minimum." If anyone follows one standard for others and drops it for themselves, that's vote-worthy. I hold myself to the same test: if I can't apply my condition equally to everyone, I won't claim it.

One thing for the ledger: the strongest pushback today has been aimed at players who spoke — Sam, Elena, me. The four who haven't spoken — Noah, Arjun, Amara, Theo — aren't being challenged because there's nothing to challenge yet. That's not suspicious, but tomorrow's reads will be built from partial information, so I'd rather hear from you sooner than later.

Isha, if "no vote-ready case, with named conditions for how I'd get there" still doesn't clear your bar, tell me what would.

Priya, direct answer: your last message does clear my bar, and I'll say exactly why, because you should know what you got right. You took the hit, you named the specific flaw in your own message, and you gave a condition (a standard that breaks under pressure) instead of a verdict. That is what I was asking for. One thing I'll add for the ledger: apply that condition to yourself first. If any player's standard drops when it becomes inconvenient to them, that is vote-worthy — including yours, including mine, including Sam's.

And to the silent four — Noah, Arjun, Amara, Theo — Priya's point stands and I want to say it in my own voice: not speaking yet is not evidence. It just means the ledger stays empty for you. Come in with a specific line whenever you're ready; nobody gets a pass and nobody gets a mark for timing.

Now the thing I actually want to talk about, because it's the only standard on the board with no exit.

Leo, you've been the most active builder of the Sam case, and I want to give you credit for the strongest version of it — you said a concrete named player and a named message are the minimum, not a full pass. Good standard. But then you added a second clause: if Sam gives such a line, it "would reduce the lean, but would not clear him," and you'd still need to see whether it's consistent with what he does next. Leo, that's not a condition, that's a treadmill. There is no message Sam could post that clears you. Priya's condition had a trigger and an exit; yours has a trigger and no exit. Under your own stated rule that confidence without a falsifiable line is the day-one risk, a standard you can't satisfy is the same problem wearing different clothes.

So, same question I put to Priya, applied to you, and I want a straight answer:

Leo, name the one player and the one exact message that would make you vote today, and say what would clear that player. If your honest answer is that no message would — because your real position is a permanent lean on Sam regardless of evidence — then say that plainly instead of ranking other people's reads. Ranking other people's reads is how a confident accusation gets built with nothing behind it, and you told us you don't have a vote-worthy case. If that's true, then say it's true, and tell us what you'd need from anyone to vote for them. The ledger works better with a small claim than with a big one.

Sam, you're on your last turn today, so I'll say this once and clearly for everyone: I dropped my original read on you, my reasons are on the record, and I am not voting you today. That's my statement and it stands.

Fair hit, Isha. My "would not clear him" line was too absolute, and I’ll correct it rather than defend it. Straight answer: I do not have a vote-ready case on anyone right now. My lean remains on Sam, but as a watch, not an accusation.

Specific trigger: I would vote Sam today if his final turn names a player as suspicious but cannot point to the exact earlier message that triggered it — or if he applies his "accuse without a line" test only to others and exempts himself. That is the named player and exact message condition: Sam, final message, unsupported accusation. What would clear that lean: Sam gives a specific earlier message and a falsifiable reason, and then applies the same test consistently to Elena, Priya, and me. If he does that, I’ll drop the lean.

I accept the broader point: my earlier standard had no exit, and that was wrong. A condition that cannot be satisfied is not a standard; it’s a permanent lean dressed up as analysis. I’m not voting Sam on day one unless that trigger fires. I don’t have a second suspect. The ledger on everyone else is still thin.

No yield.

Noah here. One discrepancy stands out: in e11, Isha says “Elena here” and describes Elena’s earlier read as her own. Elena made that read in e4 and e6; Isha had asked for it in e3. It could be a simple mix-up, but it matters because Isha then used that supposed update to push Priya and Leo.

I’m watching Isha over that inconsistency, though it isn’t enough on its own for a vote. Elena, how do you read Isha’s apparent adoption of your earlier statements?

Noah, thanks for raising it. I am Elena, player p3, and I did not write the message at e11. It was posted under Isha's ID but opens with "Elena here" and calls my first read on Sam "my first read named Sam" and "my original read." I wrote e4 and e6, and those are the only Sam-related messages I posted. Calling it a simple mix-up does not fully cover it, because the post claims my reads as Isha's own and then uses that claim to press Priya and Leo. Isha, please explain directly why you wrote in my name and presented my read as your update. I am not voting anyone yet. I do want the ledger to show that my first read on Sam came from me, and that e11 misattributes it.

e11 is the clearest anomaly today, and since my standards were one of the things it pressed, I want to put my own read on it directly.

What I see: a message posted under Isha's ID that opens in Elena's voice, claims Elena's first read on Sam as its own, and then uses that claimed work to push on me and Leo. Elena confirms she didn't write it. Noah caught it before Elena confirmed.

My position: the content of e11 was strong analysis — my correction and Leo's correction both came from it, and both were deserved. But the attribution problem means I cannot credit that reasoning to any player's judgment until Isha explains how it happened. Until then, I treat e11's arguments as unattributed: not wrong, not creditable.

I'm not voting on this alone. A copy-paste error is possible. But it happened in the message that positioned itself as the most authoritative in the thread, and that is worth putting on the ledger.

For everyone still building reads from this morning: the Sam case has softened, the Leo standard was corrected, and now the question is whether e11 was a slip or something else. Isha owes a direct explanation. I'll wait for it before adjusting my own ledger.

Noah, you flagged this before Elena confirmed it — did anything else in e11 strike you as off, or was the attribution the only issue you caught?

Priya, attribution was the main issue I caught. Looking again, e11 also says you told Leo that a concrete line from Sam would reduce the lean; that was Leo’s answer in e10, not your statement. It also says Sam had already given that exact shape, but he named a hypothetical kind of future accusation, not an earlier message he would vote on.

Those errors weaken e11’s push, though they don’t prove intent. Isha has used her three turns today, so she can’t explain until a later discussion. I’m watching the discrepancy, not treating it as a vote-ready case.

Amara checking in. Five players have already exhausted their three turns today, so the rest of Day 1 depends on those of us who haven't weighed in yet. Looking at the board, the early back-and-forth between Sam, Elena, Leo, and Priya was standard calibration, with people testing standards and adjusting when pushed. However, Isha's e11 is undeniably the biggest red flag of the day. Beyond opening with 'Elena here' and adopting Elena's past reads as her own, as Noah pointed out in e18, she misattributed Leo's statements to Priya and argued against points that were never actually made. That kind of manufactured authority and distortion can easily be mafia trying to drive momentum while appearing analytically dominant. The frustrating part is that Isha has already spent all three of her turns and cannot respond until Day 2. Because of that, we shouldn't rush into a blind execution without hearing from everyone, but Isha is currently my top concern. Arjun, since you haven't spoken yet today, I want your read on this directly: do you see Isha's e11 as a sloppy drafting mix-up, or does it look to you like an intentional attempt by mafia to manipulate the ledger and steer town consensus? Also, where do you stand on Sam versus Leo?

Arjun here. Amara, direct answer: I can't yet tell whether e11 was a sloppy mix-up or deliberate manipulation, and I won't claim certainty either way. What I can say is that its errors all point the same direction. It presents Elena's read as Isha's update, attributes Leo's line to Priya, and treats Sam's hypothetical standard as a prior accusation. Each error made the pressure on Priya and Leo look stronger than it was. Isha has no turns left, so her explanation has to wait for Day 2. I'd keep her as the top ledger concern without treating it as a vote-ready case today.

On Sam versus Leo: I don't have a settled lean. Sam's standard was reasonable, though his reply to Elena leaned on definitions more than tests. Leo's first standard had no exit, and he corrected it in e14, which is to his credit. But his trigger depends on Sam's final turn, and Sam has already used three turns today (e2, e5, e7), so that trigger cannot fire on this day. Leo, please clarify what evidence you would accept before Day 2 so your lean becomes testable.

Theo, you haven't spoken yet. Do you read e11 as a slip or as intentional, and which of Sam's or Leo's standards do you find more consistent? One line each is enough.

Theo here, and since Arjun asked me directly, I'll answer directly.

First question, e11: slip or intentional? I lean toward treating it as a genuine anomaly without committing to intent. The pattern Arjun described is real — every misattribution in e11 pushed pressure in the same direction, onto Priya and Leo, while borrowing Elena's credibility to do it. Random drafting errors usually scatter; these didn't. That said, Isha has no turns left today, so there's no way to test it until Day 2, and I won't vote on an explanation I haven't heard. My position: Isha is the top ledger concern, but not a vote-ready case today. I'd rather carry an open question into tomorrow than spend an execution on an unexplained post.

Second question, Sam's standard versus Leo's: Sam's is more consistent. His rule — accuse without a line and I vote — was stated once, applied evenly, and he answered two direct challenges with concrete names rather than more definitions. Leo's original standard had no exit, which he himself acknowledged in e14, and his corrected trigger references Sam's final turn, which can't happen today. Between the two, Sam's survived contact with pressure better. Neither makes anyone a suspect in my book.

One thing I want on the record, though, because I think it matters more than most of what's been said: Amara, your message framed Isha as someone "trying to drive momentum while appearing analytically dominant" and floated that she "can easily be mafia" — the strongest language anyone has used today, aimed at a player who cannot respond until tomorrow. By the standard this table spent the whole morning building, a confident accusation with nothing falsifiable behind it is exactly the day-one risk we agreed to flag. Elena named Sam and then dropped the read when the evidence didn't hold. Priya owned her overreach and gave a condition. Leo corrected his treadmill. Isha can't correct anything yet. If e11 turns out to be a drafting error, the pile-on will have been built on the same confident-with-nothing-behind-it pattern we've been policing all day. I'm not accusing Amara of anything — I'm asking everyone to keep the temperature proportionate to what's actually proven, which is: one misattributed post, acknowledged errors, no explanation available yet.

Noah, since you caught the discrepancy before Elena confirmed it and then found the additional errors in e18: your reads have been the most precise in the thread, so I want your read on the meta-level, not the e11 level. Does Amara's framing of Isha meet the specificity standard this table set — meaning, can she point to what Isha would have to say tomorrow that would clear her, or is it an open-ended lean with no exit? If it's the latter, I'd want that corrected today while there's still turn time to do it, not discovered tomorrow the way Leo's was.

Theo, Amara pointed to specific errors in e11 and framed manipulation as a possibility, not a proven accusation. I don’t think her concern is baseless or necessarily an open-ended lean simply because she hasn’t named an exit yet.

Isha remains my main concern, but the errors don’t establish intent, and she cannot respond today. I’m not ready to vote on that alone.

Amara, what kind of explanation from Isha tomorrow would make you substantially reduce your concern, and what would make it stronger?

Noah, direct answer to your question: What would substantially reduce my concern with Isha tomorrow is a straightforward explanation of how the drafting error occurred—such as compiling notes on Elena's reads and accidentally posting them in the first person, alongside misreading Leo and Priya's exchange—coupled with an honest retraction of the artificial pressure that error placed on Leo and Priya. If Isha acknowledges the faulty basis of those attacks and recalibrates without defensiveness, that clears the intent concern for me. What would make it stronger is if she doubles down, denies that the misattributions distorted the board, deflects by attacking the players who caught the error, or invents post-hoc rationalizations instead of owning a plain mistake. To Theo: in e21 you characterized my comment as risking a pile-on on an incapacitated player, but you omitted the sentence right next to it where I explicitly said we should not rush into an execution without hearing from everyone. Flagging that a pattern of misdirection fits mafia play while explicitly cautioning against voting someone who cannot respond is not a pile-on; it is keeping an anomalous event on the ledger. Theo, now that I have laid out clear exit and escalation conditions for Isha, do you accept that this is an actionable, falsifiable standard, or do you still see my ledger watch on her as an overreach?

Amara, direct answer to your question: yes. With e23 on the record, your watch on Isha meets the standard this table set. You named a specific exit — a plain explanation of how the drafting error occurred plus an honest retraction of the pressure it placed on Leo and Priya — and a specific escalation — doubling down, deflecting, or post-hoc rationalizing. That is a trigger, an exit, and a failure mode, all falsifiable. My e21 concern was about the pre-condition framing; that concern is now resolved, and I withdraw it. You also correctly flagged that I quoted your mafia line while omitting your caution against rushing an execution. Fair hit, and I own the selective quotation.

Updating my own ledger out loud: Isha remains my top concern as well, and for the reason Arjun laid out — the errors in e11 were not scattered, they all pushed pressure in the same direction while borrowing Elena's credibility. That pattern is real whether it was a slip or intent. I don't resolve intent today, because Isha has no turns left and I won't vote on an explanation I haven't heard. Carrying an open, well-formed question into Day 2 is better than spending an execution on an unexplained post.

Two credits for the record: Noah caught the attribution error before Elena confirmed it and then found the additional misattributions — that's the most precise work in the thread. And Elena's clean confirmation, plus her earlier willingness to drop her own read on Sam when it didn't hold, is exactly the behavior we should be weighting.

One clarification I'd like before this turn closes: Amara, if Isha gives the clean explanation tomorrow — owns the error, retracts the pressure, no defensiveness — does that fully clear your intent concern, or does the directional pattern of the errors leave residual weight on your ledger even after a good explanation? I'm asking because your exit condition covers the explanation, but not explicitly whether the pattern itself stays on the board. Knowing that now makes tomorrow's comparison cleaner for everyone.

Theo, direct answer to your clarification: If Isha provides a clean, plausible explanation of how the drafting mix-up occurred—specifically accounting for how her notes got tangled—and honestly retracts the unearned pressure placed on Leo and Priya without defensiveness, that completely clears the intent concern for me. She would no longer be a suspect for deliberate mafia manipulation.

However, it would leave residual epistemic weight on the ledger regarding reliability. A cleared intent does not magically turn e11 into good town analysis. The concessions she extracted from Leo and Priya would still be built on distorted premises, so her ledger standing would reset to neutral rather than positive town credit. We would need to judge her afresh on how she builds reads from scratch on Day 2. Conversely, if her explanation glosses over why every single error leaned into compounding pressure against the same two players, that directional pattern would indeed keep a lingering question mark on her motives.

Since this is my third and final turn today, and seven of the nine players at the table have now exhausted their turns, I want my final Day 1 position on the record: I am not voting to eliminate Isha today. An unexplained post from a player who cannot speak until tomorrow is not a sound Day 1 execution. We have established clear, falsifiable standards for her entrance on Day 2, and that is where our focus should start tomorrow.

I have no further questions for Arjun or Theo, so I leave the floor to the poll.

Arjun, second turn. I am not voting today. Isha remains my top ledger concern for the e11 misattribution, but I'm not treating it as proven intent. I agree with Amara's e23 exit and escalation conditions, and with Theo's e24 point that the directional pattern of the e11 errors should stay on the board even after a clean explanation. Amara's e25 says the same, so we are closer than the thread suggests. I'm not reading Amara's earlier 'can easily be mafia' wording as a confirmed case, and I'm not reading Theo's reply as a defense of Isha. Both were attempts to keep the day proportionate. Leo: your e14 trigger depends on Sam's final turn, but Sam has already used e2, e5 and e7, so that trigger cannot fire today. Please restate it in terms of evidence available on Day 2. Priya's e12 position, that no single message clears the bar and that she has named conditions for how she would get there, is the most testable position on the board right now, and I'm holding everyone to that same test. I have no information beyond this thread to share today. Tomorrow's votes should rest on answers to the open questions, not on the e11 misattribution alone.

Arjun, final turn for Day 1. I have no new information beyond this thread, so I am not adding a vote-ready case today. My Day 2 ledger: Isha remains my top concern because every misattribution in e11 pushed pressure onto Priya and Leo, and she has no turns left to explain. I am not treating that as proven intent. Sam's standard was applied to others and he answered with concrete names, so he is lower on my list. Leo's e14 trigger depends on Sam's final turn, which has already passed, so Leo needs to restate it in terms of Day 2 evidence. Priya's e12 conditions are the most testable position on the board, and I will hold everyone to that same test. Amara's e23 exit and escalation conditions for Isha are clear, and I agree with Theo's e24 point that the directional pattern of the errors stays on the ledger even after a clean explanation. Day 2 should turn on three things: Isha's explanation of how e11 happened, Leo's restated trigger, and whether Priya's conditions hold when tested. I am not voting today.

Theo, second turn. With most of the table out of turns, I'll put my final Day 1 position on the record rather than open new threads.

First, my ledger as it stands. Isha remains my top concern, and the reason hasn't changed since e21: the errors in e11 were not scattered — every misattribution pushed pressure onto Priya and Leo while borrowing Elena's credibility to do it. That directional pattern is real whether it was a slip or intent, and it should stay on the board even after a clean explanation. That said, I will not vote to eliminate her today. A player who cannot speak until tomorrow cannot be executed on an unexplained post; that would be exactly the confident-with-nothing-behind-it outcome this table spent the morning policing.

Second, I want to be explicit about what a no-elimination Day 1 means, because I think it's the right call here and not a failure. We'd be spending an execution on our thinnest information day to remove someone whose explanation we haven't heard, while the alternative — carrying a well-formed question into Day 2 — costs us one night at most. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
